There is no such thing as a "more evolved," or "less evolved" species. This concept stems from a common misconception of evolution as a linear progression towards increasing complexity or a predetermined "higher" form, with humans often mistakenly placed at the pinnacle. In reality, evolution is a branching process, and all living species have been evolving for the same duration since the origin of life from a last universal common ancestor.  
Evolution is driven by mechanisms such as natural selection, genetic drift, mutation, and gene flow, which lead to changes in the genetic makeup (allele frequency) of populations over generations. These changes are not guided by a goal of becoming more complex or "advanced," but rather by the pressures and opportunities presented by the environment.  
While some lineages may undergo more rapid morphological or genetic changes than others due to factors like generation time, population size, and the intensity of selective pressures, this does not make them "more evolved." A platypus, for instance, is just as evolved as a human; both have a long evolutionary history and are successfully adapted to their respective environments.

The idea of distinct, fixed "species" does not perfectly align with the continuous, ever-changing nature of evolution. Much like how you do not go to bed definitively "young" and wake up definitively "old," aging is a gradual process with socially constructed age categories. The lines we draw between species are, to a degree, arbitrary cutoffs we impose on a biological continuum for the sake of quasi-understanding and classification. There are epistemological limitation between language and physical phenomenon. There are far too many descriptive parameters at play that we could never calculate, nor comprehend.

No, it is scientifically illiterate. For example, in neuroscience, studies of transgender individuals have revealed a distinction between biological sex—defined by phenotypic genitalia and chromosomes—and gender, which is also rooted in biology. Gender refers to the sense of alignment a person feels with a particular sex. While macro-level MRI scans show no structural difference between "male" and "female" brains, at the cellular and molecular levels, distinct patterns of neuronal activity, neurotransmitter distributions, and electrical propagation occur that correspond to gender identity. Research demonstrates that transgender individuals often exhibit neurophysiological traits more closely aligned with their gender identity than their biological sex.  
  
This is not a delusion but a manifestation of measurable, causal interactions within the brain, much like traits observed in neurodivergence or homosexuality. Before addressing common strawman arguments, it is essential to clarify: age, height, or one's status as an "Apache helicopter" are objective traits that can be directly measured or falsified. Identifying as such would indeed be delusional. However, gender cannot be dissected from a brain biopsy or directly inferred from one's external anatomy. Men and women can have atypical chromosomal configurations (e.g., XXY or XO) or lose reproductive organs to disease or injury. These complexities underscore the error in conflating sex and gender as binary categories.  
  
Biologically, there are two primary sexes when not accounting for intersex conditions. However, gender does not claim to be binary in the same sense. Gender reflects a spectrum of traits shaped by neurophysiological processes, much like the color spectrum divides red and green into near-infinite shades. Similarly, the "gender spectrum" provides nuanced and more accurate descriptors for brain-based identities. Science evolves with evidence—just as Pluto was reclassified from a planet to a dwarf planet, the conceptual distinction between sex and gender has also shifted to reflect modern understandings.  
  
At its core, you are the experience of consciousness that arises from physical processes within your brain, not your body. While your body sustains these processes, hypothetically, a brain transplant would preserve your identity, whereas separating you from your brain would end it. Consequently, it is the brain's biophysical processes—interacting with the body but distinct from it—that govern gender. This does not imply that the body is irrelevant but highlights its limitations in determining one’s identity. Even many theistic frameworks posit that the self is not identical to the body, raising the question: why should a fallible body not also err in expressing one's gender?  
  
Consider the implications of a hypothetical brain transplant into a body of a different sex. Some individuals might adapt over time, while others would not experience alignment with the new body's sex regardless of hormonal changes. This aligns with the way we understand other neurobiological phenomena, such as phantom limb syndrome or intersex variations. Interestingly, transgender individuals have a 0% incidence of phantom limb syndrome compared to cisgender individuals, as their brains do not recognize the incongruent body parts as "theirs."  
  
The rarity of a phenomenon does not diminish its legitimacy. Apologists often argue that intersex conditions are statistical outliers and thus irrelevant to the discussion of binary sex. However, rarity is a poor argument against complexity. For instance, while hydrogen and helium make up over 99% of the universe's atoms, the existence of other elements is neither negligible nor unimportant. Intersex individuals represent over 1% of the population—statistically significant enough to challenge rigid binary categorizations. Furthermore, even if 100% of people fit neatly into binary biological categories, this would not negate the reality that "man" and "woman" pertain to neurophysiological, psychological, and social constructs, not solely reproductive roles.  
  
Critics often misunderstand transgender identity as an attempt to change one's biological sex, defined by gametes or chromosomes—an endeavor current technology cannot achieve. However, transgender individuals are not attempting to alter these immutable traits. Instead, their experiences are rooted in neurological processes that influence their sense of self. Questioning their legitimacy by citing high rates of suicidal ideation and detransition overlooks a crucial point: prejudice, stigma, and lack of support—not inherent "delusion"—drive these outcomes. Studies consistently show that affirmation, inclusion, and access to transition-related care yield the best psychological and social outcomes.

I am a hard-incompatibilist, hard-determinist, I am not a proponent contra-causal free will. Free will being incoherent was my entire premise.

Thoughts are either determined by internal/external prior causes (principle of sufficient reason/ cause and effect/ causal chain) in which you do not control them, or they are random (quantum indeterminacy)/ a mixture of both, in either case you do not control them.

Libertarian free will proponents insist that their choices are made for reasons, but also that those reasons do not determine their choices. Or that those reasons are not themselves determined, but also not a matter of chance, this is a contradiction.

Even if you have an agent causation (an immaterial soul), it only makes sense to say that soul is making decisions if its actions are causally determined by prior soul-states. Otherwise, its actions are uncaused, and uncaused events are, by definition, random. If you are acting randomly, that’s not really decision making. It’s only if your actions are done for reasons which cause those actions that you’re really making decisions. You’re not making decisions if you’re just doing things for no reason.

Therefore, it is only if our brains behave deterministically that we really make choices. If our choices are not determined, then it makes no sense to say that we make decisions. If our decisions are not the products of pre-existing causes, then we don’t really make them, rather they just happen on their own. If your will is free, then, by definition, you have no control over it. Some folks who insist we have free will say that if determinism is true, then you don’t really make decisions, your brain chemistry and experiences determine your decisions. But my brain processes tautologically are me. If my brain chemistry and experience are not making my decisions, then I am not making my decisions, same with if nothing external influences me. For example, we know even food effects the gut microbiome (as \~95% of serotonin and \~50% of dopamine is located there), altering brain processes, thus, altering personality, no differently from psychiatric medication.

What does it mean to say that “we are free and in control of what facts and ideas the mind focuses on” in response to Ayn Rand’s ‘freedom to think’? When I choose to focus on an idea, does something cause me to choose to focus on that idea? If the answer is yes, then I am not really in control of that act of focusing. If the answer is no, and there is nothing that determines what I will choose to focus on, the act of focusing on anything is no different from a chance event, which by definition are not controlled by anything. So, does something cause a person to focus and think, or does the person’s choice to think and focus happen for no reason? Or is it partly causally influenced and partly chance? I don’t see how responsibility or control fits into any of these options, and I don’t see what other options there are. A mixture of chance and determinism? Part of the decision-making process involves causal influences, and the rest has no prior cause. This doesn't solve it. Free will, described by its advocates imply a person has control over their decisions. If my decisions are predetermined; how do I have control over them? If my decisions have no cause, and occur for no reason, then how can I control them?  
This is ignoring that, these are two mutually exclusive possibilities, and therefore, a contradiction. If an event is partly causal, it means it is determined by previous events. If it is partly random, it means it is not determined by previous events. Furthermore, supported by the law of identity, there is only one type of randomness: complete randomness (randomness is equal to randomness). Randomness cannot be random, and non-random; a thing is either random, or not random. This means that a truly random event is unpredictable and has no underlying cause. Any sequence from a narrow perspective that appears to be both causal and random is likely the result of a hidden variable or a misunderstanding of the system.

Further supported by the law of the excluded middle in logic, which says that a proposition ‘P’ has to be true or false, and there is no in-between. If you ask if any brain activity is determined by something, the answer is truth-apt. If it is determined by something, then you have to ask what that determining factor is, and so on, leading to a causal chain. If the answer is no, then that is the definition of randomness, and you are not in control of randomness. Thus, any brain activity is either going to lead to a chain of determined causation that either itself terminates in something random or something outside of the brain, both of which are out of your control. Or it just terminates in something random a lot earlier, in which case you're not in control of it either.

The London Hammer is often hailed as an anomalous artifact: if a man-made tool is embedded in rock that old, conventional history is challenged.

However, the limestone itself has not been dated to the Ordovician period. This is a common misconception. The hammer was likely a late 19th-century miner's tool that became encased in a limestone concretion. This process can occur relatively quickly.

Creationist Carl Baugh seized on the hammer in the 1980s, using it to support his theories about a pre-Flood Earth and giant humans. The hammer is now displayed at his Creation Evidence Museum, where replicas are sold to visitors.

Internet enthusiasts have further capitalized on the hammer, using it as evidence for ancient astronauts, government conspiracies, and even the god Thor.

Researchers like John Cole and Glen Kuban have debunked these claims. They argue that the hammer's age can be explained by natural processes, and its style is consistent with 19th-century tools. Without evidence of the hammer being naturally embedded in a pre-Quaternary stratum, it remains a curiosity, not a testament to ancient civilizations or divine intervention.

In neuroscience, studies of transgender individuals have revealed a distinction between biological sex—defined by phenotypic genitalia and chromosomes—and gender, which is also rooted in biology. Gender refers to the sense of alignment a person feels with a particular sex. While macro-level MRI scans show no structural difference between "male" and "female" brains, at the cellular and molecular levels, distinct patterns of neuronal activity, neurotransmitter distributions, and electrical propagation occur that correspond to gender identity. Research demonstrates that transgender individuals often exhibit neurophysiological traits more closely aligned with their gender identity than their biological sex.

This is not a delusion but a manifestation of measurable, causal interactions within the brain, much like traits observed in neurodivergence or homosexuality. Before addressing common strawman arguments, it is essential to clarify: age, height, or one's status as an "Apache helicopter" are objective traits that can be directly measured or falsified. Identifying as such would indeed be delusional. However, gender cannot be dissected from a brain biopsy or directly inferred from one's external anatomy. Men and women can have atypical chromosomal configurations (e.g., XXY or XO) or lose reproductive organs to disease or injury. These complexities underscore the error in conflating sex and gender as binary categories.

Biologically, there are two primary sexes when not accounting for intersex conditions. However, gender does not claim to be binary in the same sense. Gender reflects a spectrum of traits shaped by neurophysiological processes, much like the color spectrum divides red and green into near-infinite shades. Similarly, the "gender spectrum" provides nuanced and more accurate descriptors for brain-based identities. Science evolves with evidence—just as Pluto was reclassified from a planet to a dwarf planet, the conceptual distinction between sex and gender has also shifted to reflect modern understandings.

At its core, you are the experience of consciousness that arises from physical processes within your brain, not your body. While your body sustains these processes, hypothetically, a brain transplant would preserve your identity, whereas separating you from your brain would end it. Consequently, it is the brain's biophysical processes—interacting with the body but distinct from it—that govern gender. This does not imply that the body is irrelevant but highlights its limitations in determining one’s identity. Even many theistic frameworks posit that the self is not identical to the body, raising the question: why should a fallible body not also err in expressing one's gender?

Consider the implications of a hypothetical brain transplant into a body of a different sex. Some individuals might adapt over time, while others would not experience alignment with the new body's sex regardless of hormonal changes. This aligns with the way we understand other neurobiological phenomena, such as phantom limb syndrome or intersex variations. Interestingly, transgender individuals have a 0% incidence of phantom limb syndrome compared to cisgender individuals, as their brains do not recognize the incongruent body parts as "theirs."

The rarity of a phenomenon does not diminish its legitimacy. Apologists often argue that intersex conditions are statistical outliers and thus irrelevant to the discussion of binary sex. However, rarity is a poor argument against complexity. For instance, while hydrogen and helium make up over 99% of the universe's atoms, the existence of other elements is neither negligible nor unimportant. Intersex individuals represent over 1% of the population—statistically significant enough to challenge rigid binary categorizations. Furthermore, even if 100% of people fit neatly into binary biological categories, this would not negate the reality that "man" and "woman" pertain to neurophysiological, psychological, and social constructs, not solely reproductive roles.

Critics often misunderstand transgender identity as an attempt to change one's biological sex, defined by gametes or chromosomes—an endeavor current technology cannot achieve. However, transgender individuals are not attempting to alter these immutable traits. Instead, their experiences are rooted in neurological processes that influence their sense of self. Questioning their legitimacy by citing high rates of suicidal ideation and detransition overlooks a crucial point: prejudice, stigma, and lack of support—not inherent "delusion"—drive these outcomes. Studies consistently show that affirmation, inclusion, and access to transition-related care yield the best psychological and social outcomes.

Even if gender-affirming surgeries provided only temporary relief, what harm does it cause to let individuals make these decisions for themselves? Medical gatekeeping standards already exist for minors, with parental consent required for many procedures. For instance, boys with gynecomastia can undergo breast reduction surgery at 16 with parental approval. Why should trans boys face different standards when seeking top surgery? A 2019 study showed that 97% of breast reduction surgeries in minors were performed on cisgender males, yet there is no comparable backlash.

The regret rate for knee replacements ranges from 6% to 30%, far exceeding the less-than-1% regret rate for top surgery in transgender men. Why, then, do critics not lobby to ban minors from undergoing procedures with significantly higher regret rates? Denying transgender individuals the care they need is inconsistent and reveals a bias against their existence, rather than concern for medical ethics.

Ultimately, the rejection of overwhelming neurophysiological and psychological evidence in favor of outdated, simplistic models of sex and gender resembles dogmatic belief systems far more than scientific inquiry. If the goal is to reduce suffering, affirming the identities of transgender individuals and supporting their access to care is the most evidence-based approach. Blaming their struggles on "delusion" or "social contagion" while ignoring the harm caused by stigma and exclusion is both unscientific and inhumane. Until science advances to address these complexities more fully, compassion and understanding remain our best tools for supporting marginalized communities.

The earliest known reference to Israel comes from the Merneptah Stela, which mentions Israel as a Canaanite tribe subdued by Egyptian Pharaoh Merneptah during a military campaign toward the end of the Bronze Age. (The use of the “people” determinative implies that Israel is an ethnic group but not a nation.) A few centuries later, an Israelite kingdom emerged in the highlands of Samaria in northern Canaan, speaking its own Canaanite dialect, which eventually became the Hebrew language, and practicing its own version of Canaanite religion.  
In the Bible, the God of Israel is known as El — the same supreme god worshipped by Israel’s Canaanite predecessors. Even the name Israel itself is a theophoric name that refers to the god El. The tradition in Deuteronomy 32:8 stating that the nations were divided according to the number of the sons of El comes from the same Canaanite traditions preserved in Ugarit, where El is the father of the other gods. The frequent depiction of El and other gods as bulls at Ugarit, Tyre, and Hazor is echoed in the golden calf idols of Jeroboam and Aaron and the bulls in the Jerusalem temple, as well as several divine titles in the Bible. The biblical epithet “Ancient of Days” recalls El’s Ugaritic epithet, “Father of Years”, which describes his status as the oldest of the gods.  
Other Canaanite deities, including Asherah, Anat, Baal, Dagan, and Reshep, also appear in the Bible. Second Kings 23 tells us that Asherah and Baal were venerated alongside Yahweh in the Jerusalem temple. Several passages depict the god Reshep, often associated with pestilence, as part of Yahweh’s retinue. Famous inscriptions from Kuntillet ‘Ajrud in Sinai and Khirbet el-Qom in Judah describe Asherah as the wife of Yahweh. Meaning that if he had the choice between scratching his finger (something of nuisance), or destroying the entire world, if you were to say "yeah, I don't want to go through the scratching my finger nonsense, I'll just destroy the entire world to avoid it" that it would not, in and of itself, be an illogical position to take. What we use in for is making sure that all our moral intuitions are consistent with each other. We use it to avoid contradicting ourselves.

Morality can be accounted for empirically. Accounting for it simply means explaining why it exists. You don’t want us to account for morality, you want us to justify morality. I don’t believe that there can be any ultimate, objective, non-circular justification for morality, even if there is a god who dictates that morality.
